claim: The PVD neuron in Caenorhabditis elegans is a multidendritic polymodal nociceptive neuron with an elaborate and organized dendritic arbor.
source: In the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, the multidendritic polymodal nociceptive neuron PVD has an elaborate and organized dendritic arbor (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 1A,B showing the PVD dendritic structure.

claim: PVD's secondary, tertiary and quaternary branches form repeated structural units resembling menorahs.
source: PVD's largely orthogonally arranged secondary (2°), tertiary (3°) and quaternary (4°) branches form repeated structural units resembling menorahs (Smith et al., 2012).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with citation to Smith et al., 2012.

claim: During development, PVD grows its entire dendrite arbor spanning 800 μm along the body in just 24 hours.
source: During development, PVD grows its entire dendrite arbor that spans 800 μm along the body of the animal in just 24 hr (Smith et al., 2010), suggestive of a high level of biosynthesis during the growth phase of this cell.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with citation to Smith et al., 2010.

claim: The rapid growth of PVD dendrites suggests a high level of biosynthesis during the growth phase.
source: During development, PVD grows its entire dendrite arbor that spans 800 μm along the body of the animal in just 24 hr (Smith et al., 2010), suggestive of a high level of biosynthesis during the growth phase of this cell.
evidence: This is an inference made by the authors based on the rapid growth rate.

claim: DMA-1 acts cell autonomously in PVD to promote dendrite branching and stabilization.
source: The formation of PVD dendrites requires a single transmembrane leucine rich repeat (LRR) protein DMA-1, which acts cell autonomously in PVD to promote dendrite branching and stabilization (Liu and Shen, 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly with citation to Liu and Shen, 2012.

claim: SAX-7/L1CAM and MNR-1 form a tripartite receptor-ligand complex with DMA-1 to guide PVD dendritic arbor growth and branching.
source: Subcellularly localized stripes of SAX-7/L1CAM, together with MNR-1 form a tripartite receptor–ligand complex and guide the growth and branching of the PVD dendritic arbor (Dong et al., 2013; Salzberg et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly with citations to Dong et al., 2013 and Salzberg et al., 2013.

claim: Two ire-1 mutant alleles (wy762 and wy782) were isolated from a forward genetic screen for mutations that alter PVD dendritic morphology.
source: From a forward genetic screen for mutations that alter the PVD dendritic morphology, we identified two loss-of-function mutations, wy762 and wy782.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text describing the experimental approach.

claim: Both ire-1 alleles (wy762 and wy782) cause dramatic loss of dendritic branches, especially in the distal dendrites of PVD.
source: Both alleles cause dramatic loss of dendritic branches, especially in the distal dendrites of PVD (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ire-1 null deletion allele ok799 shows an indistinguishable phenotype in PVD compared to wy762 and wy782.
source: In addition, a known null deletion allele of ire-1, ok799 (Henis-Korenblit et al., 2010) showed indistinguishable phenotype in PVD compared with that of wy762 and wy782 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated directly with citation and supported by Figure 1D.

claim: The complexity of the menorahs nearest to the cell body is unaffected in ire-1 mutants.
source: The complexity of the menorahs nearest to the cell body appeared unaffected in these mutants (Figure 1E), as did the morphology of PVD axon (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 1E.

claim: The morphology of PVD axon is unaffected in ire-1 mutants.
source: The complexity of the menorahs nearest to the cell body appeared unaffected in these mutants (Figure 1E), as did the morphology of PVD axon (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: FLP neurons show severe dendritic arbor defects in ire-1 mutants.
source: Interestingly, in the entire nervous system of C. elegans, the only other pair of highly branched neurons in the head region, FLP also showed severe dendritic arbor defects in ire-1 mutants (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 1H,I.

claim: Other neurons with fewer dendritic or axonal branches (IL2, VC, ADL) do not show branching defects in ire-1 mutants.
source: Other neurons with fewer dendritic or axonal branches such as IL2, VC and ADL did not show branching defects in ire-1 mutants (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: ire-1 is required for establishing highly branched dendrites.
source: Together, these results suggest that ire-1 is required for establishing highly branched dendrites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn by the authors from the experimental data.

claim: IRE-1 functions cell-autonomously in PVD to regulate dendrite morphogenesis.
source: In the ire-1 mutant background, expression of IRE-1 with a PVD-specific promoter (ser2prom3) fully restored the distal branch number and complexity of the whole dendritic arbor (Figure 1F,G) indicating that IRE-1 functions cell-autonomously in PVD to regulate dendrite morphogenesis.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: Expressing ire-1 cDNA does not cause overbranching in wild-type animals.
source: Expressing ire-1 cDNA did not cause overbranching in wild-type animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: IRE1 is conserved in all eukaryotes and contains an ER luminal domain for recognizing misfolded proteins, and cytoplasmic kinase and endoribonuclease domains.
source: IRE1 is conserved in all eukaryotes and contains an ER luminal domain for recognizing misfolded proteins in the ER, and a cytoplasmic kinase and an endoribonuclease domain, which lead to the non-conventional cytoplasmic splicing of xbp-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated directly and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The wy782 missense mutation is a substitution of a conserved residue in the kinase domain of ire-1.
source: One missense mutation (wy782) of ire-1 is a substitution of a conserved residue in the kinase domain while another missense mutation (wy762) is a substitution of a conserved residue in the endoribonuclease domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating both domains might be required for dendrite morphogenesis.
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The wy762 missense mutation is a substitution of a conserved residue in the endoribonuclease domain of ire-1.
source: One missense mutation (wy782) of ire-1 is a substitution of a conserved residue in the kinase domain while another missense mutation (wy762) is a substitution of a conserved residue in the endoribonuclease domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating both domains might be required for dendrite morphogenesis.
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both the kinase and endoribonuclease domains of IRE-1 might be required for dendrite morphogenesis.
source: One missense mutation (wy782) of ire-1 is a substitution of a conserved residue in the kinase domain while another missense mutation (wy762) is a substitution of a conserved residue in the endoribonuclease domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating both domains might be required for dendrite morphogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference made by the authors based on the location of the mutations.

claim: The kinase and endoribonuclease domains of IRE-1 are required for splicing of xbp-1 mRNA.
source: Since these two domains are required for splicing of the xbp-1 mRNA, we reasoned that the neurons should be able to bypass the requirement of IRE-1 if a spliced form xbp-1 was provided in PVD.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: PVD-specific expression of spliced xbp-1 cDNA in ire-1 mutants rescues the loss of distal dendrite branches phenotype.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, PVD-specific expression of spliced xbp-1 cDNA in ire-1 mutants rescued the loss of distal dendrite branches phenotype.
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: Expression of unspliced xbp-1 genomic DNA does not rescue the branching defect in ire-1 mutants.
source: In contrast, expression of unspliced xbp-1 genomic DNA at the same concentration did not rescue branching defect (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: Expressing spliced xbp-1 cDNA does not cause overbranching in wild type animals.
source: Expressing spliced xbp-1 cDNA did not cause overbranching in wild type animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: XBP-1 functions downstream of IRE-1 to establish complex dendritic arbor in PVD.
source: These data offer compelling evidence that XBP-1 functions downstream of IRE-1 to establish complex dendritic arbor in PVD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn by the authors from the rescue experiments.

claim: The IRE-1 arm of the UPR pathway is likely involved in dendrite morphogenesis.
source: Hence, the IRE-1 arm of the UPR pathway is likely involved in dendrite morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn by the authors from the genetic data.

claim: HSP-3 and HSP-4 are ER chaperones of the Hsp70 family homologous to mammalian grp78/BiP.
source: We searched the PVD-specific gene profiling data (Smith et al., 2010) and found that two abundant ER chaperones of the Hsp70 family (homologous to mammalian grp78/BiP), HSP-3 and HSP-4, are enriched in PVD and therefore might be the targets of XBP-1 in PVD neurons (Urano et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated directly with citations to Smith et al., 2010 and Urano et al., 2002.

claim: HSP-3 and HSP-4 are enriched in PVD neurons.
source: We searched the PVD-specific gene profiling data (Smith et al., 2010) and found that two abundant ER chaperones of the Hsp70 family (homologous to mammalian grp78/BiP), HSP-3 and HSP-4, are enriched in PVD and therefore might be the targets of XBP-1 in PVD neurons (Urano et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated directly with citation to Smith et al., 2010.

claim: Overexpression of hsp-4 in PVD restores normal dendritic branches in ire-1 mutants.
source: Consistent with this idea, overexpression of hsp-4 in PVD restored normal dendritic branches in ire-1 mutants (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Overexpression of hsp-3 does not rescue the dendritic phenotype in ire-1 mutants.
source: However, overexpression of hsp-3 or daf-21 (a cytoplasmic chaperone of the Hsp90 family) did not rescue the phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Overexpression of daf-21 does not rescue the dendritic phenotype in ire-1 mutants.
source: However, overexpression of hsp-3 or daf-21 (a cytoplasmic chaperone of the Hsp90 family) did not rescue the phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: hsp-4 single mutant does not show dendritic arbor defects.
source: Furthermore, hsp-4 single mutant did not show the dendritic arbor defects (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), indicating other ER chaperones or co-chaperones functioning in parallel with HSP-4.
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Other ER chaperones or co-chaperones function in parallel with HSP-4.
source: Furthermore, hsp-4 single mutant did not show the dendritic arbor defects (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), indicating other ER chaperones or co-chaperones functioning in parallel with HSP-4.
evidence: This is an inference made by the authors based on the lack of phenotype in hsp-4 mutants.

claim: The dendritic defect in ire-1 mutants is likely due to lack of specific chaperones in the ER.
source: These results indicate that the dendritic defect in the ire-1 mutants is likely due to lack of specific chaperones in the ER.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn by the authors from the rescue experiments.

claim: xbp-1 mutant does not show dendritic arbor defects.
source: Importantly, xbp-1 mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) did not show the dendritic arbor defects.
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Other pathways downstream of IRE-1 but independent of XBP-1 can play redundant roles in dendrite morphogenesis.
source: This suggests that other pathways downstream of IRE-1 but independent of XBP-1 can play redundant roles in dendrite morphogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference made by the authors based on the lack of phenotype in xbp-1 mutants.

claim: In the xbp-1 mutant background, somatic knockout of xrn-1 phenocopies the ire-1 dendritic phenotype in about 10% of animals.
source: Using this method, we found that in the xbp-1 mutant background, somatic knockout of xrn-1, which encodes a 5′-3′ exoribonuclease and is a key component of the 5′-3′ mRNA degradation pathway (Newbury and Woollard, 2004), phenocopied the ire-1 dendritic phenotype in PVD neurons in about 10% of the animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated directly with citation and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The RIDD pathway functions in parallel to XBP-1 to regulate dendrite branching of PVD.
source: These results indicate that the RIDD pathway functions in parallel to the XBP-1 to regulate dendrite branching of PVD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn by the authors from the somatic CRISPR experiments.

claim: atf-6 and pek-1 mutants do not show dendrite morphogenesis phenotype in PVD.
source: We also examined mutations in the other two arms of the UPR pathway, ATF-6 and PERK/PEK-1, and found that they did not show any dendrite morphogenesis phenotype in PVD (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: xbp-1 pek-1 double mutant shows a low-penetrance ire-1-like phenotype.
source: However, xbp-1 pek-1 double mutant showed a low-penetrance (about 25%) ire-1-like phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: ER homeostasis mediated by other UPR pathways also contributes to dendrite morphogenesis.
source: This suggests that the ER homeostasis mediated by other UPR pathways also contribute to dendrite morphogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference made by the authors based on the double mutant phenotype.

claim: The severe decrease of distal dendritic branches of PVD in ire-1 mutants is reminiscent of dma-1 mutants.
source: The severe decrease of distal dendritic branches of PVD in ire-1 mutants is reminiscent of dma-1 mutants.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: DMA-1 is a single transmembrane leucine-rich repeat protein prominently expressed in PVD.
source: DMA-1 is a single transmembrane leucine-rich repeat (LRR) protein prominently expressed in PVD, and mutations in dma-1 result in severely reduced dendritic branching and complexity (Liu and Shen, 2012) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated directly with citation to Liu and Shen, 2012.

claim: Mutations in dma-1 result in severely reduced dendritic branching and complexity.
source: DMA-1 is a single transmembrane leucine-rich repeat (LRR) protein prominently expressed in PVD, and mutations in dma-1 result in severely reduced dendritic branching and complexity (Liu and Shen, 2012) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated directly with citation and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DMA-1 acts in PVD as a receptor to recognize the SAX-7/L1CAM and MNR-1 ligand complex.
source: DMA-1 acts in PVD as a receptor to recognize the SAX-7/L1CAM and MNR-1 ligand complex in the surrounding skin cell to promote branching and precisely pattern the dendritic arbor (Dong et al., 2013; Salzberg et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly with citations to Dong et al., 2013 and Salzberg et al., 2013.

claim: ire-1 dma-1 double mutants show a phenotype indistinguishable from the dma-1 single mutant phenotype.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, ire-1 dma-1 double mutants showed a phenotype that is indistinguishable from the dma-1 single mutant phenotype, suggesting that these two molecules function in the same genetic pathway in dendrite morphogenesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ire-1 and dma-1 function in the same genetic pathway in dendrite morphogenesis.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, ire-1 dma-1 double mutants showed a phenotype that is indistinguishable from the dma-1 single mutant phenotype, suggesting that these two molecules function in the same genetic pathway in dendrite morphogenesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an inference made by the authors based on the double mutant phenotype.

claim: hsp-4 overexpression in ire-1 dma-1 double mutants is not able to rescue the dendritic arbor defect.
source: Furthermore, hsp-4 overexpression in ire-1 dma-1 double mutants was not able to rescue the dendritic arbor defect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that DMA-1 might be a target of HSP-4.
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: DMA-1 might be a target of HSP-4.
source: Furthermore, hsp-4 overexpression in ire-1 dma-1 double mutants was not able to rescue the dendritic arbor defect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that DMA-1 might be a target of HSP-4.
evidence: This is an inference made by the authors based on the lack of rescue.

claim: In wild type animals, GFP-tagged DMA-1 is detected on all PVD dendritic processes and at the cortex of the cell body as diffusive fluorescence.
source: In wild type animals, GFP-tagged DMA-1 was detected on all the PVD dendritic processes and at the cortex of the cell body as diffusive fluorescence.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: In wild type animals, numerous discrete intracellular puncta of DMA-1::GFP are found in the cell body and along the dendrites.
source: In addition, numerous discrete intracellular puncta were found in the cell body and along the dendrites, which presumably represent the membrane trafficking organelles that carry DMA-1 (Figure 3B) (Liu and Shen, 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly with citation and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In ire-1 mutants, the punctate DMA-1::GFP in the cell body is lost.
source: In ire-1 mutants, the punctate DMA-1::GFP in the cell body was lost (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In ire-1 mutants, somatic DMA-1::GFP co-localizes with the general ER marker cytochrome b5.
source: Instead, the somatic DMA-1::GFP in the ire-1 mutants co-localized with an general ER marker, cytochrome b5 (cb5) (Rolls et al., 2002) (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated directly with citation and shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The diffuse DMA-1::GFP signal on the distal dendrites is dramatically reduced in ire-1 mutants.
source: Moreover, the diffuse DMA-1::GFP signal on the distal dendrites was dramatically reduced in the ire-1 mutant while the signal on the proximal dendrites in ire-1 mutants was the same as in wild type (Figure 3H,J,K).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 3H,J,K.

claim: The diffuse DMA-1::GFP signal on the proximal dendrites in ire-1 mutants is the same as in wild type.
source: Moreover, the diffuse DMA-1::GFP signal on the distal dendrites was dramatically reduced in the ire-1 mutant while the signal on the proximal dendrites in ire-1 mutants was the same as in wild type (Figure 3H,J,K).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 3H,J,K.

claim: DMA-1 is trapped in the ER and is not delivered to the distal dendrite plasma membrane in ire-1 mutants.
source: These observations suggest that DMA-1 is trapped in the ER and is not delivered to the distal dendrite plasma membrane, leading to the distal dendritic phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference made by the authors based on the localization data.

claim: Overexpression of HSP-4 restores the DMA-1::GFP subcellular localization in ire-1 mutants to the normal distribution.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, overexpression of the ER chaperone HSP-4, restored the DMA-1::GFP subcellular localization in ire-1 mutants to the normal distribution (Figure 3J,K).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 3J,K.

claim: ER chaperones such as HSP-4 help to fold DMA-1, which is required for the plasma membrane localization of DMA-1 and dendrite branching.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that ER chaperones such as HSP-4 help to fold DMA-1, which is required for the plasma membrane localization of DMA-1 and dendrite branching.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn by the authors from the localization and rescue experiments.

claim: HSP-4::GFP is exclusively localized in the PVD soma.
source: Since HSP-4 is capable of folding DMA-1, we first examined the subcellular localization of HSP-4 and found that HSP-4::GFP was exclusively localized in the PVD soma (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,D), co-localizing with a rough ER marker TRAM (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G–I), HSP-4's ER localization pattern is consistent with the observation that its mammalian homolog BiP is localized in rough ER (Bole et al., 1989; Lai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: HSP-4::GFP co-localizes with the rough ER marker TRAM.
source: Since HSP-4 is capable of folding DMA-1, we first examined the subcellular localization of HSP-4 and found that HSP-4::GFP was exclusively localized in the PVD soma (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,D), co-localizing with a rough ER marker TRAM (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G–I), HSP-4's ER localization pattern is consistent with the observation that its mammalian homolog BiP is localized in rough ER (Bole et al., 1989; Lai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated directly with citations and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2G-I.

claim: The main protein synthesis and folding capacity for DMA-1 is likely in the cell body.
source: These data suggests that the main protein synthesis and folding capacity for DMA-1 is likely in the cell body.
evidence: This is an inference made by the authors based on the localization of HSP-4.

claim: In ire-1 mutants, lack of upregulation of hsp-4 by spliced XBP-1 results in less DMA-1 in the secretory pathway.
source: In ire-1 mutants, lack of the upregulation of hsp-4 by spliced XBP-1 results in less DMA-1 in the secretory pathway and insufficient diffusion of DMA-1 to the distal region might be responsible for the specific loss of distal dendrites.
evidence: This is an inference made by the authors to explain the distal dendrite phenotype.

claim: About 70% of animals overexpressing DMA-1 in ire-1 mutants show efficient rescue of the dendritic arbor.
source: Interestingly, we observed both effects: about 70% of animals showed efficient rescue of the dendritic arbor (Figure 4B,D), while about 25% of animals showed a more severe phenotype, with the loss of proximal branches in addition to the distal ones (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 4B,D.

claim: About 25% of animals overexpressing DMA-1 in ire-1 mutants show a more severe phenotype with loss of proximal branches.
source: Interestingly, we observed both effects: about 70% of animals showed efficient rescue of the dendritic arbor (Figure 4B,D), while about 25% of animals showed a more severe phenotype, with the loss of proximal branches in addition to the distal ones (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: High level of HSP-4 expression together with DMA-1 decreases the percentage of dma-1-like phenotype in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Consistent with the hypothesis, high level of chaperon HSP-4 expression together with DMA-1 decreased the percentage of dma-1-like phenotype, in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There is much less accumulation or aggregation of DMA-1::GFP in PVD cell bodies with rescued morphology compared to more severely defective animals.
source: To further test this hypothesis, we separated the transgenic animals into the phenotypically rescued animals and the severely defective animals based on their dendrite morphology, we found that there was much less accumulation or aggregation of DMA-1::GFP in the PVD cell bodies with the rescued morphology compared to more severely defective animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–G).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-G.

claim: The insufficient level of functional DMA-1 due to decreased protein folding capacity accounts for a large part of PVD dendritic defect in ire-1 mutants.
source: Together, these rescuing results argue that the insufficient level of functional DMA-1 due to decreased protein folding capacity accounts for a large part of PVD dendritic defect in the ire-1 mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn by the authors from the rescue experiments.

claim: PVD neurons are derived postembryonically during the mid-L2 larval stage.
source: PVD neurons are derived postembryonically during the mid-L2 larval stage (Sulston and Horvitz, 1977), and starting from the late L2/early L3, 2° branches begin to form followed by extension of 3° branches in the L3 stage.
evidence: This is stated directly with citation to Sulston and Horvitz, 1977.

claim: Dendrite morphogenesis in PVD is completed in the early L4 stage after 4° branches have sprouted.
source: Dendrite morphogenesis is completed in the early L4 stage after 4° branches have sprouted from the 3° branches to form a network of menorah-shaped processes (Smith et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated directly with citation to Smith et al., 2010.

claim: XBP-1::GFP is observed in the nucleus of PVD starting at the L3 stage.
source: Using this PVD specific UPR activity reporter, we observed XBP-1::GFP in the nucleus of PVD starting at the L3 stage.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: The normalized XBP-1::GFP intensity increases between L3 and late L4 animals, coincidental with the stage of rapid dendrite branch addition.
source: The normalized XBP-1::GFP intensity increased between L3 and late L4 animals, coincidental with the stage of rapid dendrite branch addition.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: The XBP-1::GFP intensity decreases in mid-adult animals.
source: The XBP-1::GFP intensity subsequently decreased in mid-adult animals (Figure 5B–K).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 5B-K.

claim: HSP-4 is a transcriptional target of activated XBP-1.
source: As an ER chaperone, HSP-4 is a transcriptional target of activated XBP-1 (Calfon et al., 2002; Urano et al., 2002), and its transcriptional level shows tight correlation with activation of the UPR with high sensitivity (Iwawaki et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated directly with citations to Calfon et al., 2002 and Urano et al., 2002.

claim: The HIS-24::GFP signal becomes clearly detectable in L3 and further increases in L4 animals during which the menorahs form.
source: We found that the HIS-24::GFP signal became clearly detectable in L3 and further increased in L4 animals during which the menorahs form.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: The HIS-24::GFP fluorescence is dramatically downregulated in adult animals.
source: The GFP fluorescence is dramatically downregulated in adult animals, (Figure 5—figure supplemental 1).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The UPR activity occurs most strongly during the time of PVD dendritic branching.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the UPR activity occurs most strongly during the time of PVD dendritic branching.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn by the authors from the developmental time course data.

claim: The normalized XBP-1::GFP fluorescence level in dma-1 knockout mutants is significantly lower compared with wild type.
source: To distinguish these models, we first tested this PVD specific UPR activity reporter in dma-1 knockout mutants and we found that the normalized XBP-1::GFP fluorescence level was significantly lower compared with wild type (Figure 6B,E,K), suggesting that a functional dma-1 gene is required to turn on the UPR activity in PVD.
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 6B,E,K.

claim: A functional dma-1 gene is required to turn on the UPR activity in PVD.
source: To distinguish these models, we first tested this PVD specific UPR activity reporter in dma-1 knockout mutants and we found that the normalized XBP-1::GFP fluorescence level was significantly lower compared with wild type (Figure 6B,E,K), suggesting that a functional dma-1 gene is required to turn on the UPR activity in PVD.
evidence: This is an inference made by the authors based on the reporter data in dma-1 mutants.

claim: Overexpression of dma-1 cDNA in PVD leads to an increase of UPR activity.
source: Conversely, overexpression of dma-1 cDNA in PVD leads to an increase of UPR activity (Figure 6H,K).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 6H,K.

claim: In dma-1 mutants, the Phsp4::HIS-24::GFP UPR activity reporter shows dramatic decrease in PVD neurons.
source: Consistently, in dma-1 mutants, another UPR activity reporter, Phsp4::HIS-24::GFP also showed dramatic decrease in PVD neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: DMA-1 is necessary for UPR induction in PVD.
source: These surprising results argue that DMA-1 is necessary for UPR induction in PVD, despite the fact that there must be many membrane proteins necessary to build dendrites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn by the authors from the reporter data.

claim: Deletion mutations in kpc-1 and hpo-30 cause severe reduction of PVD dendrites.
source: Deletion mutations in kpc-1 (a Kex2/subtilisin-like proprotein convertase and a Furin homolog) (Schroeder et al., 2013) and hpo-30 (a claudin homolog) (Smith et al., 2013) cause severe reduction of PVD dendrites.
evidence: This is stated directly with citations to Schroeder et al., 2013 and Smith et al., 2013.

claim: Neither kpc-1 nor hpo-30 mutations cause reduced UPR reporter activity in PVD.
source: While both of these gene products are processed in ER, neither mutation causes reduced UPR reporter activity in PVD (Figure 6K and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–L).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 6K and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G-L.

claim: The UPR reporter shows activity in the unbranched neuron PVC.
source: In addition, this reporter also showed activity in the unbranched neuron PVC, indicating that there might be UPR activity that is unrelated to branched dendrite morphogenesis.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: The dma-1 mutation does not change the UPR activity in PVC.
source: Nevertheless, the dma-1 mutation did not change the UPR activity in PVC (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The activation of UPR in PVD specifically depends on DMA-1 production.
source: These results demonstrate that the activation of UPR in PVD specifically depends on DMA-1 production.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn by the authors from the specificity experiments.

claim: The dendritic arbor defects in ire-1 mutants are restricted to PVD and FLP, the only two pairs of highly branched neurons in C. elegans.

claim: The physiological UPR is induced in PVD during dendrite morphogenesis.
